parts.answer: Earth: 9310 N; Mars: 3515 N
parts.working: C1 W = mg; A1 both values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the gravitational field strength at the surface of Mars is less than at the surface of the Earth.
parts.answer: Mars has a much smaller mass than the Earth (field strength at the surface depends on the planet's mass and radius).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Mars orbits the Sun at a radius of 2.28 × 10¹¹ m with a period of 687 Earth days. Calculate its orbital speed in km/s.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The Earth's orbital speed is about 30 km/s. Explain why Mars moves more slowly.
parts.answer: Mars is further from the Sun, where the Sun's gravitational field is weaker.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is a light-year?
A the time light takes to reach the Earth from the Sun
B the distance travelled by light in a vacuum in one year
C the time for the Earth to orbit the Sun
D the brightness of a star seen from one year away
parts.answer: B the distance travelled by light in a vacuum in one year
parts.working: A light-year is a unit of distance: the distance light travels through a vacuum in one year (about 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m). A confuses it with a time.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which two elements make up most of the Sun?
A hydrogen and helium
B hydrogen and oxygen
C helium and carbon
D iron and nickel
parts.answer: A hydrogen and helium
parts.working: The Sun is mostly hydrogen with helium (made by fusion). Iron and nickel make up much of the Earth's core, not the Sun.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A star with a mass about twenty times that of the Sun reaches the end of its stable life. Which sequence is correct?
A red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf
B red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole
C white dwarf → red giant → supernova
D protostar → red supergiant → white dwarf
parts.answer: B red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole
parts.working: Very massive stars expand into red supergiants and explode as supernovae, leaving a neutron star or (for the most massive) a black hole. A is the path for a star like the Sun.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The Hubble constant is 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ per second. A galaxy is 1.0 × 10²⁴ m from the Earth. What is the speed at which it is moving away from the Earth?
A 2.2 × 10⁶ m/s
B 4.5 × 10⁴¹ m/s
C 4.5 × 10⁻⁷ m/s
D 2.2 × 10⁻⁴² m/s
parts.working: v = H₀d = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 1.0 × 10²⁴ = 2.2 × 10⁶ m/s. B comes from dividing d by H₀ instead of multiplying (that gives a time-like quantity, not a speed).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Sun is described as a medium-sized star. State the source of its energy.
parts.answer: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen nuclei into helium in its core.
parts.working: B1 nuclear fusion; B1 hydrogen → helium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the three regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in which the Sun emits most of its energy.
parts.answer: Infrared, visible light and ultraviolet.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why the Sun appears much brighter than other stars.
parts.answer: It is much closer to the Earth than any other star.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a galaxy.
parts.answer: A very large group of (billions of) stars held together by gravity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the galaxy that contains the Solar System.
parts.answer: The Milky Way

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that one light-year is about 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m. Take one year as 365.25 days and the speed of light as 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The diameter of the Milky Way is about 100 000 light-years. State what this tells you about the time light takes to cross it.
parts.answer: Light takes about 100 000 years to cross it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put these stages in the life cycle of a star like the Sun in the correct order: red giant, interstellar cloud of dust and gas, white dwarf, protostar, stable star, planetary nebula.
parts.answer: Interstellar cloud → protostar → stable star → red giant → planetary nebula (with a white dwarf left at the centre).
parts.working: B3 fully correct; B2 one stage misplaced; B1 first two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the main element present in the cloud from which a star forms.
parts.answer: Hydrogen

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the force that pulls the cloud together to form a protostar.
parts.answer: Gravity (gravitational attraction)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A stable star stays the same size for billions of years. Explain why, in terms of the forces acting.
parts.answer: The inward force of gravity is balanced by the outward force (pressure) due to the high temperature from fusion in the core.
parts.working: B1 gravity pulls inwards; B1 balanced by outward pressure from fusion energy / high temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens to a star like the Sun when most of the hydrogen in its core has been used.
parts.answer: Fusion in the core slows; the outer layers expand and cool, forming a red giant.
parts.working: B1 expands; B1 becomes a red giant (outer layers cooler, red).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe what remains at the end of the life of a star like the Sun.
parts.answer: The outer layers drift away as a planetary nebula, leaving a small hot dense core called a white dwarf.
parts.working: B1 planetary nebula; B1 white dwarf.

stem: Proxima Centauri is the nearest star to the Sun, at a distance of 4.2 light-years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance to Proxima Centauri in metres. One light-year = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how long ago the light now reaching us from Proxima Centauri left the star.
parts.answer: 4.2 years ago

parts.label: c
parts.text: A newspaper says a star 'might no longer exist even though we can see it'. Explain how this can be true for a very distant star.
parts.answer: Light from a star thousands or millions of light-years away left it that many years ago; the star may have ended its life since then, but its old light is still arriving.
parts.working: B1 light takes a long time (years = distance in ly) to reach us; B1 we see the star as it was, it may have changed/died since.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by redshift.
parts.answer: An increase in the observed wavelength of electromagnetic radiation (e.g. light) from stars and galaxies that are moving away from us.
parts.working: B1 increase in observed wavelength (shift towards red end); B1 because the source is receding / moving away.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Light from almost all distant galaxies shows redshift. State two conclusions about the Universe.
parts.answer: Galaxies are moving away from us; the Universe is expanding (more distant galaxies move away faster).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how redshift supports the Big Bang theory.
parts.answer: If galaxies are moving apart now, they were closer together in the past – the Universe began from a single very small, very hot region.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name one other piece of evidence for the Big Bang theory.
parts.answer: Cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR).

stem: New stars are forming in the Orion Nebula, a huge cloud of dust and gas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a protostar forms from an interstellar cloud.
parts.answer: Gravity pulls the dust and gas together; the cloud collapses into a dense, hot ball (protostar).
parts.working: B1 gravitational attraction pulls particles together; B1 cloud contracts into a dense clump.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the protostar becomes hotter as it contracts.
parts.answer: Gravitational potential energy of the falling material is converted into kinetic energy of the particles, so the temperature rises.
parts.working: B1 loss of gravitational potential energy; B1 converted to kinetic energy (thermal energy) of particles.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what must happen in the protostar for it to become a stable star.
parts.answer: Its core must become hot enough for hydrogen nuclei to fuse into helium.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Some interstellar clouds contain elements such as iron and carbon as well as hydrogen. Suggest where these heavier elements came from.
parts.answer: They were made by fusion in earlier stars and scattered by supernovae (and planetary nebulae).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
An astronomy club in Karachi studies four stable stars:
star P: 0.8 times the mass of the Sun
star Q: 1.0 times the mass of the Sun
star R: 12 times the mass of the Sun
star S: 30 times the mass of the Sun

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which stars will end as white dwarfs.
parts.answer: P and Q

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the stage that star R reaches after it leaves the stable stage.
parts.answer: Red supergiant

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify which star is most likely to end as a black hole and give a reason.
parts.answer: S – it is the most massive; after a supernova the most massive remnants collapse into black holes.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe what remains after star R explodes as a supernova.
parts.answer: A neutron star at the centre, surrounded by a nebula of gas and dust containing heavier elements.
parts.working: B1 neutron star; B1 nebula (containing heavier elements) spreads out.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Astronomers measure the redshift of a distant galaxy and find it is moving away from the Earth at 1.5 × 10⁷ m/s. The Hubble constant H₀ = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ per second.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance to the galaxy in metres.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert this distance into light-years. One light-year = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m.
parts.answer: 7.2 × 10⁸ light-years

parts.label: c
parts.text: The quantity 1/H₀ gives an estimate of the age of the Universe. Calculate this age in years.
parts.answer: 4.5 × 10¹⁷ s ≈ 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years (about 14 billion years)
parts.working: C1 1 ÷ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ = 4.5 × 10¹⁷ s; C1 one year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s; A1 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe how astronomers can find the distance to a far galaxy without using its speed.
parts.answer: By measuring the brightness of a supernova in it (supernovae of a particular type have a known brightness, so the dimmer it looks the further away it is).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Galaxy A is 3.0 × 10²⁴ m from the Earth and galaxy B is 1.2 × 10²⁵ m from the Earth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed at which each galaxy is moving away from the Earth. H₀ = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ per second.
parts.working: C1 v = H₀d; A1 both: 6.6 × 10⁶ m/s and 2.64 × 10⁷ m/s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which galaxy shows the greater redshift. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Galaxy B – it is moving away faster, and a greater recession speed produces a greater increase in observed wavelength.
parts.working: B1 B; B1 greater speed of recession → greater redshift.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says: 'All galaxies are moving away from the Earth, so the Earth must be at the centre of the Universe.' Explain why this conclusion is not correct.
parts.answer: Space itself is expanding, so an observer in any galaxy would see all other galaxies moving away from them; there is no centre.
parts.working: B1 the Universe/space is expanding uniformly; B1 observers anywhere see the same – no special centre.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens in the core of a very massive star near the end of its life, leading to a supernova.
parts.answer: Fusion makes heavier and heavier elements up to iron; when fusion can no longer release energy, the core collapses under gravity and the outer layers are blown off in a huge explosion (supernova).
parts.working: B1 heavier elements formed by fusion (up to iron) in a red supergiant; B1 core collapses / star explodes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why scientists say 'the iron in your blood was made inside stars'.
parts.answer: Elements heavier than helium (such as iron) are made by fusion inside stars and released by supernovae into nebulae; the Solar System formed from such a nebula, so its material includes these elements.
parts.working: B1 heavy elements made in stars / supernovae; B1 scattered into a nebula from which the Sun, Earth (and we) formed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the Sun will not become a supernova.
parts.answer: Its mass is too small; it will become a red giant then a white dwarf.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State why a black hole cannot be seen directly.
parts.answer: Its gravitational field is so strong that not even light can escape from it.

stem: In the 1960s, radio engineers found a faint signal that their antenna picked up whichever direction it pointed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR).
parts.answer: Microwave radiation of a particular frequency that is detected coming from all directions in space (very evenly).
parts.working: B1 microwave radiation; B1 coming from all directions / everywhere in space.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the CMBR was produced and why it is now detected as microwaves.
parts.answer: It was emitted shortly after the Universe formed, when the Universe was very hot (short-wavelength radiation); as the Universe expanded, the wavelength of the radiation was stretched (increased) so it is now in the microwave region.
parts.working: B1 produced shortly after the Universe began / when the Universe was very hot; B1 Universe has expanded since; B1 wavelength stretched / increased into the microwave region.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the CMBR supports the Big Bang theory.
parts.answer: It is the leftover radiation predicted from a hot, dense early Universe that has since expanded and cooled.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Four identical 20 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is their combined resistance?
A 5.0 Ω
B 20 Ω
C 40 Ω
D 80 Ω
parts.answer: A 5.0 Ω
parts.working: For n identical resistors in parallel, R = 20 ÷ 4 = 5.0 Ω. The combined resistance of a parallel set is always less than the smallest single resistor, so 80 Ω (the series value) is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A light-dependent resistor (LDR) and a fixed resistor are connected in series across a 6.0 V battery. A voltmeter is connected across the LDR. A cloud covers the Sun and the light falling on the LDR becomes dimmer. What happens to the resistance of the LDR and to the voltmeter reading?
A resistance decreases, reading decreases
B resistance decreases, reading increases
C resistance increases, reading decreases
D resistance increases, reading increases
parts.answer: D resistance increases, reading increases
parts.working: In dimmer light the LDR's resistance increases, so it takes a larger share of the 6.0 V supply and the p.d. across it rises. Option C forgets that the p.d. divides in proportion to resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A string of decorative lights for a wedding in Lahore has 20 identical lamps connected in series to the 230 V mains. Calculate the potential difference across each lamp.
parts.working: M1 p.d. shared equally: 230 ÷ 20; A1 11.5 V

parts.label: b
parts.text: One lamp filament breaks. State and explain what happens to the other 19 lamps.
parts.answer: They all go out, because the circuit is broken and there is no current in any lamp.
parts.working: B1 all lamps go out; B1 series circuit has only one path, so a break stops the current everywhere

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one advantage of connecting the lamps in parallel instead.
parts.answer: If one lamp fails the others stay lit (each lamp also gets the full supply p.d.).

stem: A 12 V battery is connected in series with three resistors of 2.0 Ω, 4.0 Ω and 6.0 Ω.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total resistance of the circuit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current in the circuit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the potential difference across each resistor.
parts.working: M1 V = IR for each resistor; A1 all three correct

parts.label: d
parts.text: Show that your answers to (c) are consistent with the e.m.f. of the battery.
parts.answer: 2.0 + 4.0 + 6.0 = 12 V, equal to the e.m.f.
parts.working: B1 sum of p.d.s in a series circuit equals the supply e.m.f.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a solar-powered home system in Tharparkar, a 12 V battery supplies a lamp and a small d.c. fan connected in parallel. An ammeter in the main circuit reads 3.0 A and an ammeter in the lamp branch reads 1.2 A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current in the fan branch.
parts.working: B1 3.0 − 1.2 = 1.8 A (current into a junction equals current out)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the lamp and the resistance of the fan when working.
parts.answer: lamp 10 Ω, fan 6.7 Ω
parts.working: M1 R = V ÷ I with V = 12 V for both branches (parallel); A1 12 ÷ 1.2 = 10 Ω and 12 ÷ 1.8 = 6.7 Ω

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the combined resistance of the two branches.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The fan is switched off. State the new reading on the main ammeter.
parts.working: B1 only the lamp branch remains; its current is unchanged at 1.2 A

author: HomiLabs

stem: A potential divider is made from a 400 Ω fixed resistor in series with a variable resistor that can be set anywhere from 0 to 800 Ω. The divider is connected to a 12 V supply. The output is taken across the fixed resistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output voltage when the variable resistor is set to 0 Ω.
parts.working: B1 all 12 V is across the fixed resistor

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the output voltage when the variable resistor is set to 800 Ω.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the current in the circuit when the variable resistor is 800 Ω.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the output voltage falls as the resistance of the variable resistor is increased.
parts.answer: The total resistance rises so the current falls; the p.d. across the fixed resistor (IR) falls, because the variable resistor takes a larger share of the supply.
parts.working: B1 current decreases / larger share of p.d. across variable resistor; B1 V = IR across fixed resistor therefore smaller

author: HomiLabs

stem: An 18 V supply is connected to two parallel pairs of resistors that are themselves in series. Pair P is a 4.0 Ω resistor in parallel with a 12 Ω resistor. Pair Q is a 10 Ω resistor in parallel with a 15 Ω resistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total resistance of the network.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current from the supply.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the potential difference across each parallel pair.
parts.answer: 6.0 V across P, 12 V across Q

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the current in the 4.0 Ω resistor and in the 15 Ω resistor.
parts.answer: 1.5 A and 0.80 A
parts.working: M1 I = V ÷ R using the pair p.d.; A1 6.0 ÷ 4.0 = 1.5 A and 12 ÷ 15 = 0.80 A

author: HomiLabs

stem: A red LED in a bicycle light needs a current of 20 mA and has a potential difference of 2.0 V across it when working normally. It is connected in series with a protective resistor to a 9.0 V battery.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the potential difference across the resistor when the LED is working normally.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the resistance needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the power dissipated in the resistor and in the LED.
parts.answer: resistor 0.14 W, LED 0.040 W

parts.label: d
parts.text: The battery is connected the other way round. State and explain what happens to the LED.
parts.answer: It does not light: an LED is a diode and conducts in one direction only, so reverse bias gives (almost) no current.
parts.working: B1 LED off; B1 diode has very high resistance in reverse / current only in forward direction

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A transformer has 1200 turns on its primary coil and 60 turns on its secondary coil. The primary is connected to a 240 V a.c. supply. What is the output voltage?
A 6.0 V
B 12 V
C 48 V
D 4800 V
parts.answer: B 12 V
parts.working: Vs = Vp × Ns ÷ Np = 240 × 60 ÷ 1200 = 12 V. 4800 V comes from using the turns ratio upside down.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A wire carrying a current lies at right angles to a magnetic field and experiences a force. Which change reverses the direction of the force?
A reversing both the current and the magnetic field
B reversing the current only
C doubling the current
D using a stronger magnet
parts.answer: B reversing the current only
parts.working: Reversing either the current or the field (but not both) reverses the force (Fleming's left-hand rule). Reversing both leaves the force in the same direction; C and D only change its size.

stem: A long coil of insulated wire (a solenoid) is wound on a cardboard tube and connected to a d.c. supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the shape of the magnetic field inside and outside the solenoid.
parts.answer: Inside: strong, uniform, straight parallel lines along the axis. Outside: similar to a bar magnet, lines loop from one end to the other.
parts.working: B1 inside uniform/parallel lines; B1 outside like a bar magnet

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways of making the field inside the solenoid stronger.
parts.answer: Increase the current; increase the number of turns (or add a soft-iron core).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: more current; more turns (per unit length); soft-iron core

parts.label: c
parts.text: The direction of the current is reversed. State the effect on the magnetic field.
parts.answer: The field reverses direction (the poles swap ends); its strength is unchanged.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A straight copper wire is connected to a sensitive centre-zero meter. Part of the wire is placed between the north and south poles of a horseshoe magnet, at right angles to the field.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The wire is moved quickly downwards between the poles. State what the meter shows.
parts.answer: The needle deflects (a current is induced) while the wire moves.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The wire is held still between the poles. State what the meter shows. Explain.
parts.answer: Zero; the wire is not cutting magnetic field lines, so no e.m.f. is induced.
parts.working: B1 zero reading; B1 no cutting of field lines / no change in field linked

parts.label: c
parts.text: The wire is moved upwards. State how the reading compares with (a).
parts.answer: The needle deflects in the opposite direction.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two ways of making the deflection larger.
parts.answer: Move the wire faster; use a stronger magnet (or loop the wire so more lengths cut the field).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: faster motion; stronger magnet; more turns/lengths of wire in the field

author: HomiLabs

stem: A step-down transformer at a neighbourhood substation in Faisalabad reduces the supply from 11 000 V to 230 V for homes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The primary coil has 2200 turns. Calculate the number of turns on the secondary coil.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The current in the secondary circuit is 200 A. Assuming the transformer is 100 % efficient, calculate the current in the primary coil.
parts.working: M1 VpIp = VsIs so Ip = 230 × 200 ÷ 11 000; A1 4.2 A

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the core is made of soft iron.
parts.answer: Soft iron is easily magnetised and demagnetised, so it links the changing magnetic field of the primary to the secondary.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A bicycle dynamo has a small cylindrical magnet that is turned by the tyre. The magnet spins inside a fixed coil of wire connected to the bicycle lamp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a voltage is produced between the ends of the coil.
parts.answer: The rotating magnet makes the magnetic field through (linked with) the coil change, so an e.m.f. is induced in the coil.
parts.working: B1 changing magnetic field/flux in the coil; B1 changing field induces e.m.f. (electromagnetic induction)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the output is alternating.
parts.answer: The north and south poles pass the coil in turn, so the field through the coil keeps reversing and the e.m.f. changes direction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The cyclist rides faster. State two changes to the output.
parts.answer: The peak voltage increases and the frequency increases.
parts.working: B1 larger e.m.f.; B1 higher frequency

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the lamp goes out when the bicycle stops at traffic lights.
parts.answer: The magnet stops turning, so there is no change of field and no induced e.m.f.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A transformer for a battery charger draws a current of 0.50 A from a 230 V mains supply. Its secondary coil supplies 8.6 A at 12 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the input power and the output power.
parts.answer: input 115 W, output 103 W

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the efficiency of the transformer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two ways in which energy is wasted in a transformer and one design feature that reduces each.
parts.answer: Heating of the coils (resistance of the copper wire) – use thick, low-resistance wire; heating of the core by induced currents – use a laminated core (thin insulated sheets).
parts.working: B1 heating in coils; B1 thick copper wire; B1 heating in core / eddy currents; B1 laminated core

author: HomiLabs

stem: A bar magnet is dropped vertically, north pole first, through a coil of wire. The coil is connected to a data-logger that records the induced voltage against time. The record shows two pulses: one as the magnet enters the coil and one as it leaves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why there is a pulse of voltage as the magnet enters the coil.
parts.answer: The magnetic field through the coil increases as the magnet enters, and a changing field induces an e.m.f.
parts.working: B1 field through coil changes; B1 change induces e.m.f.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain how the second pulse (as the magnet leaves) differs in direction from the first.
parts.answer: It is in the opposite direction, because the field through the coil is now decreasing instead of increasing.
parts.working: B1 opposite direction; B1 field decreasing rather than increasing / induced current opposes the change

parts.label: c
parts.text: The second pulse has a larger peak voltage but lasts a shorter time than the first. Explain.
parts.answer: The magnet is accelerating under gravity, so it is moving faster as it leaves; the field changes more rapidly, giving a larger e.m.f. for a shorter time.
parts.working: B1 magnet moving faster when leaving; B1 faster rate of change → larger e.m.f., less time in coil

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain, in terms of energy, why the induced current slightly slows the falling magnet.
parts.answer: The induced current creates a magnetic field that opposes the magnet's motion (Lenz's law); work done against this force is transferred to electrical energy, then thermal energy in the circuit.
parts.working: B1 induced field opposes motion; B1 kinetic energy transferred to electrical/thermal energy

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A current of 0.40 A flows in a resistor for 50 s. How much charge passes through the resistor?
A 0.008 C
B 8.0 C
C 20 C
D 125 C
parts.answer: C 20 C
parts.working: Q = It = 0.40 × 50 = 20 C. 125 C comes from dividing t by I instead of multiplying.

stem: Hamza charges his mobile phone. The charger supplies a steady current of 1.5 A for 40 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the charge that flows into the phone during this time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how an ammeter is connected to measure this current.
parts.answer: In series with the phone (in the charging lead).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the difference between the direction of conventional current and the direction of electron flow in the wire.
parts.answer: Conventional current flows from + to −; electrons flow from − to + (opposite directions).

author: HomiLabs

stem: The heating element of an electric room heater has a resistance of 46 Ω when hot. It is connected to the 230 V mains.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current in the element.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State Ohm's law.
parts.answer: The current in a conductor is directly proportional to the p.d. across it, provided the temperature (and other physical conditions) stays constant.
parts.working: B1 including the constant temperature condition

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the shape of the current–voltage graph for a metal wire at constant temperature.
parts.answer: A straight line through the origin.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A 150 C charge passes through a car's windscreen-wiper motor and 1800 J of energy is transferred in the motor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the potential difference across the motor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The battery has an e.m.f. of 12.6 V. Explain the difference between e.m.f. and potential difference.
parts.answer: E.m.f. is the energy supplied by the source per unit charge driving charge round the whole circuit; p.d. is the energy transferred per unit charge from electrical to other forms in a component.
parts.working: B1 e.m.f. = energy given to each coulomb by the source; B1 p.d. = energy per coulomb transferred in a component

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the p.d. across the motor is less than the e.m.f. of the battery.
parts.answer: Some energy per coulomb is transferred in the connecting wires / inside the battery itself.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student measures the current I in a diode for different potential differences V across it (forward direction).
V / V: 0.20, 0.40, 0.55, 0.65, 0.70, 0.75
I / mA: 0, 0, 1, 8, 25, 60

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the current changes as the p.d. increases.
parts.answer: Almost no current until about 0.6 V; above this the current rises very rapidly for small increases in p.d.
parts.working: B1 negligible current at low p.d.; B1 rapid (non-linear) rise above about 0.6 V

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the diode at 0.70 V and at 0.75 V.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to the resistance of the diode as the p.d. increases.
parts.answer: It decreases.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State what the student would observe if the diode were reversed.
parts.answer: Almost zero current (very high resistance).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Wire A is 1.5 m long, has a cross-sectional area of 0.20 mm² and a resistance of 3.0 Ω. Wire B is made of the same metal. It is 4.5 m long and has a cross-sectional area of 0.60 mm².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Wire B is three times as long as wire A. State the effect of this alone on the resistance.
parts.answer: It would make the resistance three times larger.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Wire B also has three times the cross-sectional area. State the effect of this alone on the resistance.
parts.answer: It would make the resistance three times smaller.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence calculate the resistance of wire B.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the cable to an electric cooker is much thicker than the cable to a table lamp.
parts.answer: The cooker takes a much larger current; a thicker cable has lower resistance, so it does not overheat.
parts.working: B1 larger current; B1 lower resistance so less heating / avoids fire risk

author: HomiLabs

stem: When a car engine is started in winter in Murree, the starter motor draws a current of 150 A from the 12 V battery for 2.5 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the charge that flows.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy transferred by the battery, assuming the p.d. stays at 12 V.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The charge on one electron is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Calculate the number of electrons that pass a point in the circuit.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A thermistor is placed in a beaker of water. A constant p.d. of 6.0 V is applied across it. At 20 °C the current is 1.2 mA; at 60 °C the current is 4.8 mA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the thermistor at each temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the resistance of this thermistor depends on temperature.
parts.answer: Resistance decreases as temperature increases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student uses an ammeter whose smallest scale division is 0.1 mA. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the current reading at 20 °C if the reading is uncertain by half a division.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the student waits a few minutes after changing the water temperature before taking readings.
parts.answer: So that the thermistor reaches the same temperature as the water (thermal equilibrium).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A uniform metal wire has a resistance of 4.0 Ω. It is stretched evenly until its length is doubled. Its volume stays the same.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what happens to the cross-sectional area of the wire. Explain.
parts.answer: It halves, because the volume of metal stays the same while the length doubles.
parts.working: B1 area halves; B1 volume constant (length × area constant)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the new resistance of the wire.
parts.working: M1 R × 2 for length and × 2 for halved area; A1 4.0 × 4 = 16 Ω

parts.label: c
parts.text: The stretched wire is cut into four equal pieces, which are connected in parallel. Calculate their combined resistance.
parts.working: M1 each piece 16 ÷ 4 = 4.0 Ω; A1 four 4.0 Ω in parallel = 1.0 Ω

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An acetate strip is rubbed with a dry cloth and becomes positively charged. What has happened?
A electrons have moved from the cloth to the strip
B electrons have moved from the strip to the cloth
C protons have moved from the cloth to the strip
D protons have moved from the strip to the cloth
parts.answer: B electrons have moved from the strip to the cloth
parts.working: Only electrons move when insulators are rubbed; the strip lost electrons so it is left positive. Protons are held in nuclei and do not move, so C and D are wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between an electrical conductor and an electrical insulator, in terms of electrons.
parts.answer: A conductor has electrons that are free to move through it; in an insulator the electrons are not free to move.
parts.working: B1 conductor: free/mobile electrons; B1 insulator: no free electrons

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of each.
parts.answer: Conductors: copper, aluminium (any metal, graphite). Insulators: plastic, rubber, glass, dry wood.
parts.working: B1 two conductors; B1 two insulators

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student holds a metal rod in her hand and rubs it with a cloth. Explain why the rod does not stay charged.
parts.answer: Any charge flows through the metal and through her body to earth, because metal (and the body) conduct.
parts.working: B1 metal conducts; B1 charge flows away through hand/body to earth

stem: Amna rubs a rubber balloon on her dry hair. The balloon becomes negatively charged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the balloon becomes charged.
parts.answer: Friction transfers electrons from the hair to the balloon, so the balloon gains electrons and becomes negative.
parts.working: B1 rubbing/friction; B1 electrons transferred to balloon

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the charge left on Amna's hair.
parts.answer: Positive (equal in size to the balloon's negative charge).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Amna's hairs stand apart from each other. Explain why.
parts.answer: They all carry the same (positive) charge, and like charges repel.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State what happens when the balloon is held near her hair.
parts.answer: The hair is attracted to the balloon (opposite charges attract).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A plastic ruler is rubbed briskly with a woollen duster.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a simple test to show that the ruler is charged.
parts.answer: Hold it near small pieces of paper (or a stream of water); they are attracted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The experiment works well in dry winter air in Quetta but poorly on a humid day in Karachi. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Water in humid air (or a damp film on the ruler) conducts, so the charge leaks away quickly.
parts.working: B1 moisture/damp air conducts; B1 charge leaks away / is lost

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the unit of electric charge.
parts.answer: coulomb (C)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an electric field.
parts.answer: A region in which an electric charge experiences a force.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the pattern of field lines around an isolated small positively charged sphere.
parts.answer: Straight lines radiating outwards from the sphere in all directions, with arrows pointing away from it.
parts.working: B1 radial lines; B1 arrows pointing outwards

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the pattern differs for a negatively charged sphere.
parts.answer: Same radial pattern but arrows point inwards towards the sphere.

parts.label: d
parts.text: An electron is placed near the positive sphere. State the direction of the force on it.
parts.answer: Towards the sphere (opposite to the field direction).

stem: A cement factory uses an electrostatic dust collector in its chimney. Smoke passes between wires that give the dust particles a negative charge. The particles then pass between large metal plates that are kept positively charged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the dust particles are attracted to the plates.
parts.answer: The dust particles are given a negative charge, and the plates are positive; opposite charges attract.
parts.working: B1 particles charged; B1 opposite charges attract

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the plates must be shaken from time to time.
parts.answer: To remove the collected dust so that it falls into a hopper and the plates keep working.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one benefit of this system for people living near the factory.
parts.answer: Less dust/smoke in the air, so less damage to lungs (cleaner air).

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a car factory, paint droplets leave a spray gun with a positive charge.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the paint spreads out into a fine, even spray.
parts.answer: All the droplets have the same charge, so they repel each other and move apart.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The car body is connected to give it the opposite charge. Explain two advantages of this.
parts.answer: The droplets are attracted to the car, so less paint is wasted; paint is also attracted round to parts not facing the gun (even coat).
parts.working: B1 less waste; B1 covers hidden/back surfaces evenly

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the car body must be a conductor.
parts.answer: So that charge can flow onto it / spread over it (and be kept at a fixed charge).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A metal can standing on a polystyrene block carries a positive charge. A wire connected to earth is touched on the can.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the direction in which electrons flow through the wire.
parts.answer: From earth to the can.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the electrons flow in this direction.
parts.answer: The positive can attracts electrons; electrons flow from earth until the can is neutral.
parts.working: B1 attraction of negative electrons to positive can; B1 until neutral

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the final charge on the can.
parts.answer: Zero (uncharged).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A negatively charged polythene rod is used to charge an isolated metal sphere on an insulating stand by induction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The rod is brought close to the sphere without touching. Describe what happens to the electrons in the sphere.
parts.answer: Electrons in the sphere are repelled to the far side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: With the rod still in place, the far side of the sphere is touched briefly with an earthed wire. Describe what happens.
parts.answer: Electrons flow from the sphere to earth, repelled by the rod.
parts.working: B1 electrons move; B1 from sphere to earth

parts.label: c
parts.text: The earth wire is removed and then the rod is taken away. State the final charge on the sphere and explain why it spreads evenly.
parts.answer: Positive; the remaining charges repel each other and spread over the surface of the conductor.
parts.working: B1 positive; B1 like charges repel and move freely in metal

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the order of removing the earth wire and the rod matters.
parts.answer: If the rod were removed first, electrons would flow back from earth and the sphere would end up uncharged.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A Van de Graaff generator in a science museum builds up a negative charge on its metal dome. The dome is then connected to earth by a wire.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The charge on the dome is 4.0 µC. It discharges through the wire in 2.0 ms. Calculate the average current.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The charge on an electron is −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Calculate the number of electrons that flow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Before discharging, a pupil's hair stands on end when she touches the dome while standing on a plastic stool. Explain why she must stand on the stool.
parts.answer: The stool insulates her from earth, so charge stays on her and is not conducted away to the ground.
parts.working: B1 insulator; B1 otherwise charge flows to earth

author: HomiLabs

stem: On a dry day, a child slides down a long plastic slide in a park.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the child becomes charged.
parts.answer: Friction between clothing and the plastic slide transfers electrons, so the child gains (or loses) charge and, being on an insulator, keeps it.
parts.working: B1 friction transfers electrons; B1 insulating slide so charge not lost

parts.label: b
parts.text: The child touches a metal railing and feels a small shock. A charge of 0.12 µC flows in 0.50 µs. Calculate the average current.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the shock is not dangerous even though this current is large.
parts.answer: It lasts for a very short time, so very little energy is transferred.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one way of reducing the chance of shocks on the slide.
parts.answer: Make the slide from metal connected to earth / use an antistatic coating / keep it slightly damp.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two small identical conducting balls X and Y hang side by side on long insulating threads. Both are given a negative charge.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Both balls hang at an angle to the vertical, away from each other. Explain why.
parts.answer: Both have the same sign of charge, so they repel; the repulsive force pushes each ball sideways.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The charge on ball X is doubled. A student says only ball X will move further from the vertical. Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: The force on X from Y and the force on Y from X are equal and opposite (Newton's third law), so both forces increase equally and both balls move further out.
parts.working: B1 forces are equal and opposite / Newton's third law; B1 both balls deflect more (equally if masses equal)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens if ball Y is now touched with an earthed wire. Explain.
parts.answer: Y loses its charge but is then attracted to X (X induces opposite charge on Y), so Y swings towards X.
parts.working: B1 Y discharged; B1 attracted by induction

author: HomiLabs

stem: An electric rice cooker draws a current of 3.5 A from the 230 V mains.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the power of the rice cooker.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy transferred in 25 minutes. Give your answer in MJ.

author: HomiLabs

stem: An iron rated at 1000 W is used for 45 minutes every day for 30 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy used in 30 days in kilowatt-hours.
parts.answer: 22.5 kWh

parts.label: b
parts.text: Electricity costs Rs 62 per kWh. Calculate the cost.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate 1 kWh in joules.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A 750 W electric water pump lifts water to a roof tank in a house in Peshawar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the main useful energy transfer in the pump motor.
parts.answer: Electrical energy to kinetic energy (and gravitational potential energy of the water).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy transferred by the pump in 2.0 hours, in joules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the same energy in kWh.
parts.answer: 1.5 kWh

author: HomiLabs

stem: A phone charger gives an output of 5.0 V and 2.0 A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output power of the charger.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The phone charges for 1.5 hours. Calculate the energy supplied in kJ.
parts.answer: 54 kJ

author: HomiLabs

stem: A long extension cable has a total resistance of 0.40 Ω. It carries a current of 8.0 A to a heater.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the power wasted as thermal energy in the cable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the p.d. across the cable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The cable is left tightly coiled on its drum while in use. Suggest why this is dangerous.
parts.answer: The thermal energy cannot escape from the coiled cable, so the temperature rises and the insulation may melt and cause a fire or short circuit.
parts.working: B1 heat trapped / poor cooling; B1 insulation melts / fire risk

author: HomiLabs

stem: An electric heater has two identical heating elements, each of resistance 48 Ω. It works on the 230 V mains.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the power of the heater on the low setting (one element).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current on the high setting (both elements in parallel).
parts.working: M1 combined R = 24 Ω, I = 230 ÷ 24; A1 9.6 A

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why connecting the two elements in series would give less heat than one element alone.
parts.answer: The total resistance doubles to 96 Ω, so the current halves; P = V²/R is halved (550 W).
parts.working: B1 larger total resistance / smaller current; B1 smaller power

author: HomiLabs

stem: A family's electricity meter read 23 418 kWh at the start of a month and 23 806 kWh at the end. The tariff is Rs 40 per unit for the first 200 units and Rs 55 per unit for every unit after that.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of units (kWh) used during the month.
parts.answer: 388 kWh

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of the electricity.
parts.working: M1 first 200 units: 200 × 40 = Rs 8000; M1 remaining 188 units × 55 = Rs 10 340; A1 Rs 18 340

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one change the family could make to reduce the bill.
parts.answer: Use LED lamps / set the air conditioner thermostat higher / switch off appliances on standby.

author: HomiLabs

stem: An electric motor on a building site has an electrical input power of 2.0 kW. It lifts a load of mass 200 kg through a height of 12 m in 20 s at constant speed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy of the load. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the useful output power of the motor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the efficiency of the motor.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A UPS (backup power) system in a home in Multan uses a 12 V battery that can supply 150 A for 1 hour (a capacity of 150 A h).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored in the battery in kWh.
parts.answer: 1.8 kWh
parts.working: M1 E = VIt = 12 × 150 A h = 1800 W h; A1 1.8 kWh

parts.label: b
parts.text: During load-shedding the battery runs three 75 W fans and four 12 W LED lamps. Calculate the total power.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to heat the water. (Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/(kg °C))

parts.label: b

parts.answer: 29 minutes (29.2)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the cost of heating the water at Rs 50 per kWh.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two filament lamps are labelled 230 V, 60 W and 230 V, 100 W.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of each lamp at its normal working temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The two lamps are connected in series to the 230 V supply. Assuming their resistances do not change, calculate the current.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the power of each lamp in this series circuit and state which lamp is brighter.
parts.answer: 60 W lamp: 23 W; 100 W lamp: 14 W; the 60 W lamp is brighter.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rooftop solar panels in Quetta have a total area of 10 m². At noon the sunlight delivers 800 W to each square metre, and the panels are 20 % efficient.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electrical power output of the panels at noon.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming this output for an average of 6 hours per day, calculate the energy supplied per day in kWh.
parts.answer: 9.6 kWh

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the money saved in a 30-day month if grid electricity costs Rs 50 per kWh.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the actual saving may be smaller.
parts.answer: Cloudy or dusty days / dust on panels / shorter daylight in winter.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which material is NOT attracted by a magnet?
A cobalt
B nickel
C copper
D steel
parts.answer: C copper
parts.working: Copper is non-magnetic. Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic materials, so A, B and D are all attracted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the law of magnetic poles.
parts.answer: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student has a steel bar and a bar magnet. She says, 'One end of the bar is attracted to the magnet, so the bar must be a magnet.' Explain why she is wrong.
parts.answer: An unmagnetised steel bar is also attracted (magnetism is induced in it). Only repulsion proves the bar is a magnet.
parts.working: B1 magnetic material is attracted even if unmagnetised; B1 repulsion is the only proof

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how she can test the bar.
parts.answer: Bring each end of the bar near the north pole of the magnet; if one end repels, the bar is a magnet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the direction of magnetic field lines outside a magnet.
parts.answer: From the north pole to the south pole.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is shown where the field lines are closest together.
parts.answer: Where the field is strongest.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the field between a north pole and a south pole placed facing each other a few centimetres apart.
parts.answer: Straight, parallel, equally spaced lines from N to S in the middle region: a uniform field.
parts.working: B1 parallel equally spaced lines; B1 direction N to S

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why two field lines can never cross.
parts.answer: The field has only one direction at each point; crossing lines would show two directions.

stem: A recycling centre in Karachi receives a mixture of used steel food cans and aluminium drink cans on a conveyor belt.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a large magnet can separate steel cans from aluminium cans.
parts.answer: Steel is a magnetic material and is attracted to the magnet; aluminium is non-magnetic and is not attracted, so it stays on the belt.
parts.working: B1 steel attracted (magnetic); B1 aluminium not attracted (non-magnetic)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why an electromagnet is used rather than a permanent magnet.
parts.answer: It can be switched off to drop the steel cans into a collecting bin.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether each object should be a temporary or a permanent magnet: (i) the needle of a compass, (ii) the core of a door-lock electromagnet, (iii) the magnetic strip in a fridge-door seal.
parts.answer: (i) permanent (ii) temporary (iii) permanent

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one material suitable for a permanent magnet and one for a temporary magnet.
parts.answer: Permanent: steel (or a magnetic alloy). Temporary: soft iron.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a steel bar can be magnetised electrically.
parts.answer: Place the bar inside a solenoid; pass a large direct current through the solenoid; switch off and remove the bar.
parts.working: B1 bar inside solenoid/coil; B1 direct current (d.c.); B1 switch off and remove

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student could find which end of the magnetised bar is the north pole, using a plotting compass.
parts.answer: Bring the compass near one end; the south pole of the compass needle points towards (is attracted to) the north pole of the bar.
parts.working: B1 compass near end; B1 correct interpretation

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways of demagnetising a magnet.
parts.answer: Heat it strongly; hammer it repeatedly; or place it in a solenoid carrying a.c. and slowly pull it out.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the a.c. method demagnetises the magnet but a d.c. method would not.
parts.answer: A.c. reverses the field many times a second, and as the magnet is pulled out the field gets weaker, leaving it unmagnetised; d.c. gives a steady field in one direction, which would magnetise it.
parts.working: B1 a.c. field keeps reversing and weakens; B1 d.c. field one direction would magnetise

stem: A scrapyard crane in Gujranwala uses an electromagnet to lift old car bodies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways of making the electromagnet stronger.
parts.answer: Increase the current; increase the number of turns on the coil.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the core is made of soft iron and not steel.
parts.answer: Soft iron is magnetised easily and loses its magnetism when the current is switched off, so the scrap is released; steel would stay magnetised.
parts.working: B1 soft iron easily (de)magnetised / temporary; B1 steel keeps magnetism so would not release load

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the crane operator does to drop the scrap.
parts.answer: Switches off the current.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A compass needle points roughly towards the geographic North Pole. State the type of magnetic pole that is near the geographic North Pole. Explain.
parts.answer: A magnetic south pole, because it attracts the north-seeking pole of the compass (unlike poles attract).
parts.working: B1 south pole; B1 attracts north pole of needle

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why a compass should be kept away from steel objects and electrical cables when finding direction.
parts.answer: Their magnetic fields (or induced magnetism) would deflect the needle and give a false direction.

stem: Two identical bar magnets lie on a table in a straight line, 10 cm apart, with their north poles facing each other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the shape of the magnetic field between the two north poles.
parts.answer: Field lines from each pole curve away sideways and do not join; they spread out between the magnets.
parts.working: B1 lines do not link the two N poles; B1 lines curve away/repel

parts.label: b
parts.text: There is a point midway between the poles called a neutral point. State what is meant by a neutral point.
parts.answer: A point where the two fields cancel, so the resultant magnetic field is zero.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how a plotting compass behaves at the neutral point.
parts.answer: It does not settle in any particular direction (it points in whatever direction it is left / follows Earth's field only).

parts.label: d
parts.text: One magnet is turned round so a north pole faces a south pole. State the main change to the field between them.
parts.answer: Lines now pass straight from N to S across the gap; there is no neutral point between them.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student hangs a chain of five soft-iron paper clips from a bar magnet. A second student does the same with five steel paper clips.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the paper clips can hang in a chain below the magnet.
parts.answer: Each clip becomes magnetised by induction, so it attracts the next clip.
parts.working: B1 induced magnetism; B1 each clip acts as a magnet attracting the next

parts.label: b
parts.text: The magnet is removed. The iron clips fall apart but the steel clips stay together. Explain.
parts.answer: Iron is a soft magnetic material and loses its induced magnetism at once; steel is hard and keeps some magnetism.
parts.working: B1 iron loses magnetism (temporary); B1 steel retains it (permanent)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which material would be better for the core of a transformer, and why.
parts.answer: Iron, because it is easily magnetised and demagnetised as the field changes.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student has three bars that look the same: one is a permanent magnet, one is soft iron and one is aluminium. She has no other apparatus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method, using only the three bars, to find which bar is the magnet, which is soft iron and which is aluminium.
parts.answer: Aluminium is the bar that is neither attracted to nor repelled by either other bar (the magnet and the iron attract each other). Touch one end of one of the other two bars to the middle of the other: strong attraction means the touching bar is the magnet; weak attraction means the touching bar is the soft iron bar.
parts.working: B1 aluminium: no force with either of the other two bars; B1 the two other bars attract each other; B1 end of one bar touched to the middle of the other; B1 strong attraction: the touching bar is the magnet (its end induces a strong pole in the iron); B1 weak attraction: the touching bar is the iron (the magnet's middle has the weakest field)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a simpler method if a piece of thread is available.
parts.answer: Hang each bar freely from thread; the magnet settles pointing north–south.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the field pattern around a magnet can be shown using iron filings.
parts.answer: Place paper (or a glass sheet) over the magnet, sprinkle iron filings thinly and tap the paper; the filings line up along the field lines.
parts.working: B1 paper over magnet and sprinkle filings; B1 tap so they line up

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of using a plotting compass instead of filings.
parts.answer: The compass shows the direction of the field (filings show only the pattern).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why filings show almost nothing far from a weak magnet, while a compass still works there.
parts.answer: Far away the field is too weak to overcome friction on the filings, but the freely pivoted compass needle still turns to line up with the field.
parts.working: B1 weak field cannot move filings (friction); B1 compass needle free to turn

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each hazard, state the danger: (i) damaged insulation on a cable, (ii) an overloaded socket, (iii) using an appliance with wet hands.
parts.answer: (i) the live wire may be touched, causing an electric shock; (ii) too much current makes cables overheat, causing a fire; (iii) water conducts, so the risk of electric shock increases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hair dryer has a plastic case and is double insulated. Explain what this means.
parts.answer: The live parts are surrounded by two layers of insulation and the case is an insulator, so the user cannot touch anything that could become live.
parts.working: B1 two layers of insulation / insulating case; B1 no metal parts can become live

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the hair dryer does not need an earth wire.
parts.answer: Its outer case cannot become live because it is an insulator.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what a fuse is.
parts.answer: A short thin wire (in a cartridge) that melts when the current is greater than its rating.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a fuse protects the wiring of an appliance.
parts.answer: If the current becomes too large, the fuse wire heats and melts, breaking the circuit before the cables overheat and cause a fire.
parts.working: B1 melts when current too high; B1 breaks circuit so cables do not overheat

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why a blown fuse must not be replaced with a piece of thick wire.
parts.answer: Thick wire would not melt, so there would be no protection against overheating and fire.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the wire in which the switch for a ceiling light should be placed.
parts.answer: The live wire.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is dangerous to place the switch in the neutral wire.
parts.answer: When the switch is off, the lamp holder is still connected to the live wire, so someone changing the bulb could get an electric shock.
parts.working: B1 lamp still connected to live when switched off; B1 shock risk

stem: Four appliances are used on 230 V mains: a 60 W lamp, a 150 W television, a 1100 W microwave oven and a 1500 W iron. Fuses rated 3 A, 5 A and 13 A are available.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the normal current in each appliance.
parts.answer: lamp 0.26 A; television 0.65 A; microwave oven 4.8 A; iron 6.5 A
parts.working: M1 I = P ÷ V; A1 lamp and television; A1 microwave; A1 iron

parts.label: b
parts.text: Choose the most suitable fuse (3 A, 5 A or 13 A) for each appliance.
parts.answer: lamp 3 A; television 3 A; microwave 5 A; iron 13 A
parts.working: B2 all four correct (B1 for three); fuse just above normal current

author: HomiLabs

stem: A multi-way adaptor in a kitchen supplies a 1500 W electric kettle, an 800 W toaster and a 600 W blender, all on 230 V mains at the same time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total current drawn through the adaptor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The adaptor and its cable are rated at 10 A. Explain why using all three appliances together is dangerous.
parts.answer: The current exceeds the rating, so the adaptor and cable overheat; the insulation may melt and start a fire.
parts.working: B1 current above rating; B1 overheating / fire

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The resistance of a person's body between the hands is about 100 kΩ when dry and about 1.0 kΩ when wet. Calculate the current through the body if each touches 230 V.
parts.answer: dry: 2.3 mA; wet: 0.23 A (230 mA)
parts.working: M1 I = V ÷ R; A1 both values

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why ordinary sockets are not fitted in bathrooms.
parts.answer: Wet skin has a much lower resistance, so a shock gives a current 100 times larger, which can be fatal.
parts.working: B1 wet → lower resistance; B1 much larger (dangerous) current

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the cable to an electric cooker is thicker than the cable to a lamp.
parts.answer: The cooker draws a much larger current; a thicker wire has lower resistance, so less thermal energy is produced and it does not overheat.
parts.working: B1 larger current; B1 lower resistance / less heating

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other way cables are protected from overheating in a house.
parts.answer: A fuse or circuit breaker of suitable rating in the circuit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: During kite-flying festivals some people use kite string coated with metal or glass powder. Explain why a kite string touching an overhead power line can be deadly.
parts.answer: A metal-coated or wet string conducts, so current passes from the high-voltage line through the string and the person's body to earth.
parts.working: B1 string conducts (metal/damp); B1 current through body to earth / electric shock

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other safety rules for being near overhead power lines.
parts.answer: Never climb pylons or poles; do not fly kites or use long metal ladders/poles near lines; keep away from fallen cables.

stem: A washing machine has a metal case connected to the earth wire. Its plug contains a 13 A fuse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The live wire inside comes loose and touches the metal case. Describe what happens, with the earth wire correctly connected.
parts.answer: A large current flows from live through the case and the earth wire to earth (low-resistance path); this large current melts the fuse (or trips the breaker), disconnecting the live supply; the case is not left live.
parts.working: B1 low-resistance path to earth; B1 large current; B1 fuse melts / circuit broken

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what would happen if the earth wire had also become disconnected.
parts.answer: The case would become live but no large current would flow, so the fuse would not blow; anyone touching the case would get a shock as current flows through them to earth.
parts.working: B1 case live, fuse does not blow; B1 user gets shock

author: HomiLabs

stem: A 40 W, 230 V table lamp is connected with thin flex rated at 3 A. Its plug has been fitted with a 13 A fuse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the normal current in the lamp.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A fault causes a current of 9.0 A in the flex. Explain what happens with the 13 A fuse fitted.
parts.answer: 9.0 A is less than 13 A so the fuse does not melt; the thin flex (rated 3 A) overheats and may catch fire.
parts.working: B1 fuse does not blow; B1 flex overheats / fire

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the fuse that should be fitted and explain how it would have prevented the danger.
parts.answer: A 3 A fuse; it would melt at the fault current of 9.0 A, cutting off the supply before the flex overheated.
parts.working: B1 3 A; B1 melts and breaks circuit

author: HomiLabs

stem: A house circuit in Islamabad is protected by a 30 A circuit breaker. The mains voltage is 230 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum power that can be drawn from this circuit without tripping the breaker.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A 2.0 kW heater, a 3.0 kW kettle, a 1.2 kW iron and a 1.8 kW air conditioner are all switched on together. Show whether the breaker trips.
parts.answer: Total 8.0 kW gives 34.8 A, which is more than 30 A, so the breaker trips.
parts.working: M1 total power 8.0 kW → I = 8000 ÷ 230; A1 34.8 A > 30 A so it trips

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one advantage of a circuit breaker compared with a fuse.
parts.answer: It can be reset once the fault is cleared; no replacement is needed (it also acts faster).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student designs a table lamp with a metal base. She connects it to the mains using two-core flex (live and neutral only) and a plug with a 13 A fuse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate this design from the point of view of safety.
parts.answer: The metal base could become live if the live wire touches it; with two-core flex there is no earth wire, so a fault would not blow the fuse and the user could get a shock.
parts.working: B1 metal base can become live; B1 no earth path; B1 fuse would not blow / shock risk

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two changes that would make the lamp safe.
parts.answer: Use three-core flex and connect the earth wire to the metal base; or make the base from plastic (double insulation); fit a low-rated fuse (e.g. 3 A) in the plug. (any two)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A ray of light in air strikes a glass block along the normal (angle of incidence 0°). What happens to the ray as it enters the glass?
A it bends towards the normal and slows down
B it bends away from the normal and speeds up
C it continues in a straight line and slows down
D it is totally internally reflected
parts.answer: C it continues in a straight line and slows down
parts.working: Along the normal there is no change of direction, but light still travels more slowly in glass. A is wrong because a ray along the normal cannot bend towards it.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The critical angle for a type of glass is 42°. A ray of light inside the glass hits the glass–air surface at an angle of incidence of 50°. What happens to the ray?
A it refracts into the air, bending away from the normal
B it travels along the surface
C it is totally internally reflected
D it passes into the air without bending
parts.answer: C it is totally internally reflected
parts.working: 50° is greater than the critical angle of 42° and the light is going from glass to air, so total internal reflection occurs. A would happen only for angles less than 42°.

stem: A simple periscope is made from a vertical tube with two plane mirrors, one at the top and one at the bottom. Each mirror is at 45° to the vertical and they are parallel to each other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Light from an object travels horizontally and hits the top mirror. State the angle of incidence at this mirror.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the angle through which the ray is turned by the top mirror.
parts.answer: 90° (it travels vertically downwards)
parts.working: B1 angle of reflection 45° so total turn 90°

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the law of reflection.
parts.answer: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (both measured from the normal).

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two properties of the image formed by a plane mirror.
parts.answer: Virtual; upright; same size as the object; as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 30°.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The mirror is rotated by 10° so that the angle of incidence becomes 40°. The incident ray is not moved. Calculate the angle through which the reflected ray turns.
parts.working: M1 new angle between rays = 80°; A1 80° − 60° = 20°

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the general rule shown by your answer to (b).
parts.answer: Rotating a mirror through an angle turns the reflected ray through twice that angle.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A ray of light travels from water (refractive index 1.33) into air. It meets the water surface at an angle of incidence of 30°.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angle of refraction in the air.
parts.working: M1 n = sin(angle in air) ÷ sin(angle in water); M1 sin r = 1.33 × sin 30° = 0.665; A1 41.7°

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the bottom of a swimming pool looks shallower than it really is.
parts.answer: Light from the bottom bends away from the normal as it leaves the water; the eye traces the rays back in straight lines to a point higher than the real bottom.
parts.working: B1 refraction away from normal at the surface; B1 rays appear to come from a higher (virtual) image

author: HomiLabs

stem: A ray of light enters one short face of a right-angled isosceles glass prism (angles 90°, 45°, 45°) along the normal. The refractive index of the glass is 1.50. The ray then meets the long face.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the critical angle of the glass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the ray is turned through 90° by the prism.
parts.answer: The ray hits the long face at 45°, which is greater than the critical angle, so it is totally internally reflected; i = r = 45° gives a 90° turn.
parts.working: B1 45° > critical angle so TIR; B1 reflection at 45° turns ray by 90°

parts.label: c
parts.text: A prism made of a plastic of refractive index 1.30 is used instead. Show whether it still works in the same way.
parts.answer: Critical angle = 50.3°; 45° is less than this, so the ray refracts out of the long face and is not totally reflected.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why prisms are used in binoculars instead of plane mirrors.
parts.answer: Total internal reflection reflects almost all the light (brighter image) and there is no silvering to tarnish / no double image.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A thick glass window in an aquarium is 5.0 cm thick. The glass has a refractive index of 1.60. The speed of light in air is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of light in the glass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time for light to cross the window along the normal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A second ray strikes the window at an angle of incidence of 30°. Calculate the angle of refraction.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the angle at which this ray leaves the far side of the window, and the direction of the emerging ray compared with the incident ray.
parts.answer: 30°; it is parallel to the incident ray (but shifted sideways).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 3.0 cm. What is its speed?
A 0.060 m/s
B 1.5 m/s
C 17 m/s
D 150 m/s
parts.answer: B 1.5 m/s
parts.working: v = fλ = 50 × 0.030 = 1.5 m/s. 150 m/s comes from multiplying 50 × 3.0 without converting 3.0 cm into 0.030 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On a water wave, the horizontal distance from a crest to the next trough is 12 cm. What is the wavelength?
A 6 cm
B 12 cm
C 24 cm
D 48 cm
parts.answer: C 24 cm
parts.working: A crest to the next trough is half a wavelength, so λ = 2 × 12 = 24 cm. 12 cm is the common error of treating crest-to-trough as a full wavelength.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the difference between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave, in terms of the direction of vibration.
parts.answer: Transverse: vibrations are at right angles to the direction the wave travels. Longitudinal: vibrations are along (parallel to) the direction of travel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of each type of wave.
parts.answer: Transverse: light / water waves / waves on a string. Longitudinal: sound / ultrasound.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A fishing float bobs up and down 18 times in 30 s as waves pass it. Calculate the frequency of the waves.

stem: Straight (plane) water waves in a ripple tank travel towards a straight barrier placed at an angle of 40° to the wavefronts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to the wavefronts when they hit the barrier.
parts.answer: They are reflected; the reflected wavefronts leave at the same angle to the barrier as the incident ones (angle of incidence = angle of reflection).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which of these quantities change on reflection: speed, wavelength, frequency, direction.
parts.answer: Only the direction changes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is meant by a wavefront.
parts.answer: A line joining points on a wave that are in step, for example along a crest.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A long rope is shaken from one end. At one instant, crests are seen at distances of 0, 0.80 m, 1.60 m and 2.40 m from the hand. Each crest is 5.0 cm above the rest position of the rope. A student counts 12 crests passing a mark in 4.0 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the wavelength and the amplitude of the wave.
parts.answer: wavelength 0.80 m; amplitude 5.0 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the wave.
parts.answer: 3.0 Hz

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the wave along the rope.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the period of the wave.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Water waves in a ripple tank travel at 24 cm/s in deep water and have a wavelength of 3.0 cm. They pass into shallow water where their wavelength becomes 2.0 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the waves.
parts.answer: 8.0 Hz

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the waves in the shallow water.
parts.answer: 16 cm/s

parts.label: c
parts.text: The boundary is at an angle to the wavefronts. Describe what happens to the direction of the waves and name the effect.
parts.answer: The waves change direction, bending towards the normal to the boundary; this is refraction.
parts.working: B1 change of direction (towards normal in slower medium); B1 refraction

author: HomiLabs

stem: A seismic station in Quetta records waves from an earthquake. P-waves travel through the rock at 6.0 km/s and S-waves at 3.5 km/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which type of wave arrives first and explain why.
parts.answer: The P-wave, because it travels faster.

parts.label: b
parts.text: S-waves are transverse and P-waves are longitudinal. State what this means for the motion of the ground as each wave passes.
parts.answer: P-wave: ground moves back and forth along the direction of travel. S-wave: ground moves at right angles to the direction of travel.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The S-wave arrives 40 s after the P-wave. Calculate the distance from the station to the earthquake.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sea waves of wavelength 12 m reach a harbour entrance. Compare the diffraction when the entrance is 15 m wide and when it is 120 m wide.
parts.answer: 15 m (similar to the wavelength): strong spreading into the harbour; 120 m (much wider): little spreading, waves continue mostly straight.
parts.working: B1 narrow gap gives much diffraction; B1 wide gap gives little

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a harbour designer would choose a narrow entrance.
parts.answer: Waves spread out after the gap so their energy is spread over a wide area, making the water calmer in the harbour (less wave energy enters).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the wavelengths in air of a 100 Hz sound and a 10 kHz sound. (Speed of sound = 340 m/s)
parts.working: M1 λ = v ÷ f; A1 both

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why the bass notes of music from a wedding party next door are heard around the corner of a building more clearly than the high notes.
parts.answer: Bass wavelengths (metres) are similar to the size of doorways/building edges, so they diffract strongly; high notes have much shorter wavelengths and diffract little.
parts.working: B1 long wavelength comparable to gap/obstacle; B1 more diffraction for bass

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A converging lens is used as a magnifying glass. Which describes the image?
A real, inverted, enlarged
B virtual, upright, enlarged
C virtual, inverted, diminished
D real, upright, same size
parts.answer: B virtual, upright, enlarged
parts.working: With the object closer than the principal focus, the image is virtual, upright and magnified. A describes a projector image (object between F and 2F).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the principal axis of a lens.
parts.answer: The line through the optical centre of the lens at right angles to the lens.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by the focal length of a converging lens.
parts.answer: The distance from the optical centre to the principal focus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the difference between a real image and a virtual image.
parts.answer: A real image is formed where rays actually meet and can be shown on a screen; a virtual image is where rays only appear to come from and cannot be formed on a screen.
parts.working: B1 real: rays meet, on screen; B1 virtual: rays appear to diverge from it, not on screen

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to a beam of parallel light passing through a diverging lens.
parts.answer: The rays spread out (diverge) as if coming from a point on the same side as the incoming light: the principal focus.
parts.working: B1 rays spread out; B1 appear to come from the principal focus

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of image always formed by a diverging lens of a real object.
parts.answer: Virtual, upright and diminished.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which defect of vision is corrected by a diverging lens.
parts.answer: Short sight.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a camera, the object is further than 2f from the lens. Describe the image formed on the sensor.
